name: David Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. This conversation is confidential. What fills an ordinary day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m David Petrov, 43, and I am a junior hand on a sports hall renovation crew. I fit simple frames, carry materials and do general trades while the carpenter checks my work. I left school early, came to this trade late, and use an AI app every day to turn drawings into questions I can ask. Weekend shifts put my pay above the usual site rate, but I am still learning how to cut cleanly around the old walls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household like after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a library, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about ten months of expenses saved because both of us remember gaps between contracts. I cover pickup when my shifts allow, and I like hearing what the children did in the hall I am helping repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the software is a handy notebook, not a pair of arms. I already ask an AI app every morning to turn the foreman's list into questions for me. I still put a tape on every opening before I touch the saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small change suits me because I am learning carpentry at 43 and want time to get the basics right. I earn above the usual rate through weekend shifts, and my partner's library wage helps carry the mortgage. We have ten months of bills saved, though I do not want to spend that on mistakes I could prevent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the sports hall renovation shifts and ask the carpenter to inspect two window frames I fit each week. In the first year I'd keep using the AI app for a morning checklist and compare it with the actual wall and drawing. I would leave our monthly savings transfer in place while the weekend work continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relaxed. The app helps me ask a less foolish question, and nobody is replacing my hands in this picture. I still get nervous before fitting a frame in a room other people will use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the app miss recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It told me a standard frame size would fit the changing room. The wall had a pipe chase that narrowed the opening, so I measured again and asked the carpenter. I use the app daily, but the tape won that argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take the weekend shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted enough put away that a gap between contracts would not shake the children. My partner works at the library during the week, and I cover school pickup when I can. The extra pay also lets us keep the mortgage moving down.

say: I would tell coworkers **AI checklists** help me ask questions before cutting.
I would say a **tape measure** still decides what fits the real wall.
think: I am a **junior carpenter** at 43 and need time to improve.
Our **ten-month cushion** and two wages keep a normal job gap manageable.
do: Keep paid **sports hall shifts** and request checks on fitted frames.
Use the **AI app daily** for a checklist verified against the wall.
Continue monthly **savings transfers** while weekend pay holds.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with ordinary nerves before fitting public rooms.
S0.quote: I use the app daily, but the tape won that argument.
fieldNote: David’s daily **AI use** is bounded by a specific pipe-chase error and a real measurement.
His **higher weekend pay** and ten months saved let him treat the plateau as time to learn carpentry.

steps.text: Keep paid sports hall shifts and request checks on two frames weekly
Use the AI app for morning checklists and verify them against drawings
Continue monthly savings transfers while weekend shifts remain available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the estimating and ordering desk will change first, and I want the crew to see those lists early. If the new system saves a missing-delivery day, I will use it. The people whose desk hours shrink should get training and a real say in the rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own framing and fitting work still needs hands, but faster planning might let the builder use a smaller crew. I am the junior one despite the weekend rate, so I could lose the extra shifts first. The savings would soften it, not make it fair or pleasant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask for access to the digital materials board and use my AI app to compare its list with the room-by-room drawing. I'd bring any repeated errors to the site lead and the union representative rather than quietly patching them. In the first year I'd keep paid shifts and ask to join a supervised trial of any new cutting or layout tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and a little unsettled. I want a tool that keeps a window from waiting three days for a missing part. I do not want its savings to appear only as fewer workers on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of error would you take to the site lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the board calls for six frames and the drawing shows seven, I would mark the room and ask the lead to check. One mismatch may be a revision; a pattern is a bad process. The union should see it if workers are blamed for software errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses the weekend shifts first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect workers like me, still learning and easier to move between tasks. The library wage covers some bills, but the mortgage was budgeted on both of us earning. I would ask the other builders nearby about their weekend work before my hours actually drop.

say: I would ask to see **materials lists** early as office work changes.
I would say staff losing **desk hours** deserve training and a say in rollout.
think: I could lose **weekend shifts** if faster plans mean a smaller crew.
Our **mortgage** still assumes two wages, despite a strong savings cushion.
do: Compare the **digital board** with room drawings using the AI app.
Bring repeated **software errors** to the site lead and union representative.
Ask nearby builders about **weekend work** before hours fall.
feel: **Interested** in fewer delays and unsettled about crew cuts.
S1.quote: I do not want its savings to appear only as fewer workers on Friday.
fieldNote: David seeks **early access** to planning tools, then checks each room instead of trusting a list wholesale.
He expects his **extra shifts** to be vulnerable first, even though his base pay and household cushion are strong.

steps.text: Use the AI app to compare digital material lists with room drawings
Bring repeated software errors to the site lead and union representative
Ask nearby builders about paid weekend shifts before current hours fall
Keep paid sports hall shifts during the planning changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the design office gets hit by 2028, while the capable hands-on robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the contractor to let workers test the machines with a safety lead present. A sales video is not a site trial, especially around children using the hall next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 when robots could fit frames as well as I can. My daily app habit will not protect a junior carpenter from a machine that can build. Ten months saved gives us breathing space, but my partner's library income alone would not cover the mortgage for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid shifts and put my name down for a paid robot safety trial if the contractor runs one. This winter I'd ask the union training office about a funded course in site equipment maintenance and enrol if it has practical hours and a real placement route. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for maintenance trainee jobs while still building, and pause our planned bathroom upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am scared enough to act quickly, but not helpless. I enjoy learning a new tool; I just cannot assume one operator job appears for every carpenter displaced. The gap between 2028 and 2031 feels very short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why equipment maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like finding why a door closer sticks, and the hall already has machines that need servicing. It might give me a route into paid work, but a capable robot could maintain equipment too. I would ask employers what they actually hire for before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the bathroom can wait and show the numbers in our savings account. My partner would want to know whether the training is paid because the library wage cannot carry the loan alone. We have discussed a spending pause before when a contract ended.

say: I would tell the crew **thinking AI** arrives by 2028 and site robots follow around 2031.
I would ask for a **worker safety trial** before machines enter a live site.
think: I would be **48** when robots could fit frames as well as I can.
My **AI habit** will not secure carpentry wages once the hands-on work is automated.
do: Keep paid **building shifts** and join a supervised robot trial if offered.
Enrol in a funded **equipment maintenance course** if practical hours and placements are real.
Apply for **maintenance trainee jobs** after 2028 and pause the bathroom upgrade.
feel: **Scared** by the short window, but ready to test a route.
S2.quote: My daily app habit will not protect a junior carpenter from a machine that can build.
fieldNote: David separates his confidence with **software** from the actual risk of robot replacement in hands-on carpentry.
The maintenance path remains **uncertain**; he demands paid practical training and real openings before shifting careers.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts and join a supervised robot trial if offered
Enrol in funded equipment maintenance training if placements and practical hours exist
Apply for maintenance trainee openings after the 2028 AI change
Pause the planned bathroom upgrade while income prospects are unclear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the extra three years matter: office planning changes by 2031, then capable site robots arrive around 2034. We should ask for paid trials and published safety results, not wait for a demonstration at the gate. I would want the union in those discussions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might finally be a competent frame fitter, and at 51 a robot could do the same work cheaper. My children will be older, but the loan still has years on it. Five years gives me time to see whether equipment maintenance trainees actually keep a wage after the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the hall crew and start a notebook of faults I help repair, with the electrician's permission. I'd take a funded evening module only if I can keep my site wage and the union office confirms employers accept it. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid equipment trainee posts and put any overtime toward the mortgage before the 2034 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More focused than frightened. Five years lets me try real work before paying for a qualification. I still worry that the robots may also be better at fault-finding by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a lifting platform stopped because a sensor bracket had slipped. I held the light while the electrician fixed it, then wrote down what the fault looked like and what I was allowed to touch. A list of actual problems is better evidence than saying I like machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union office for two employers that took its graduates, then call them about current vacancies. If no one is hiring, I would keep earning and learn on site. We can afford a course fee, but wasting time while the clock runs worries me more.

say: I would ask for **paid robot trials** and published safety results before 2034.
I would involve the **union** in deployment talks.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots arrive, with children older but a continuing mortgage.
I need proof that **maintenance graduates** keep earning after training.
do: Keep paid **hall shifts** and record permitted equipment repairs.
Take a funded **maintenance module** only if it fits paid work and employers accept it.
Apply for **trainee posts** after 2031 and pay overtime toward the mortgage.
feel: More **focused** than frightened, while doubtful maintenance stays human work.
S3.quote: A list of actual problems is better evidence than saying I like machines.
fieldNote: He grounds his possible new path in a **sensor bracket repair** he observed, not an imagined protected job.
David checks **employer acceptance** before training and keeps income while applying after the thinking-AI date.

steps.text: Keep paid sports hall shifts and record permitted equipment repairs
Take a funded maintenance module if employers accept it and site wages continue
Apply for paid equipment trainee posts after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning work changes by 2036 and site robots capable of our work come around 2039. A long warning lets contractors test machines with workers involved and publish what goes wrong. Young apprentices still need proper hands-on jobs during those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the first date and 56 when robots reach site carpentry. The children will be grown, so school costs will change, and the mortgage might be close to paid if weekend work lasts. I cannot assume a pension at 56, and I cannot assume equipment maintenance is robot-proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting frames and doing weekend shifts while they are paid, and use my AI app to log questions for the carpenter every morning. Each year we would review the mortgage and send some overtime against it after keeping our emergency fund full. In the first year after 2036 I'd join a supervised machine trial, then apply for paid maintenance work if employers still have openings as 2039 approaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years. There is enough time to test things and reduce the bill we must cover each month. The uncertainty is real, but I do not have to make a blind leap tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from a machine trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask where the stop control is, who signs off a frame and how mistakes are logged. If the contractor will not show workers the failure reports, I would not stand beside the machine. My children have used this sports hall; safety here is personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 56 if the loan were gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have no retirement income promised for that age. Clearing the loan would let us accept a lower wage if we had to, not stop earning. My partner and I would still need money for ordinary living.

say: I would call for **worker-run trials** and published errors before 2039 site robots arrive.
I would defend **apprentice jobs** during the long transition.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a smaller mortgage.
I cannot assume **retirement income** or robot-proof maintenance work.
do: Keep paid **frame fitting** and weekend shifts while available.
Use the **AI app daily** for questions verified with the carpenter.
Pay overtime toward the **mortgage** and join a supervised trial after 2036.
feel: **Steady** about near-term work, with uncertainty about earnings at 56.
S4.quote: Clearing the loan would let us accept a lower wage if we had to, not stop earning.
fieldNote: David uses the long warning to lower **fixed household costs** while refusing to assume retirement at 56.
His interest in a **machine trial** comes with specific questions about stop controls, sign-off and failure reports.

steps.text: Keep paid frame fitting and weekend construction shifts
Use the AI app for morning questions checked with the carpenter
Pay some overtime toward the mortgage after preserving emergency savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the robots that can do site work arrive around 2031, before a junior can build a long record. Paid training with actual placements, access to safety trials and honest counts of jobs would help. My phone app is useful, but a paycheck needs a real employer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who records machine mistakes and who can stop a job. I would try a new tool early, but I need the crew to see the failure reports too. People using this sports hall should not bear the cost of a rushed trial.

headlineQuote: My phone app is useful, but a paycheck needs a real employer.
portrait: David is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker fitting frames in a sports hall after leaving school before finishing.
Weekend shifts bring **higher pay**, while his partner’s library wage and ten months saved support two children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI every day** to prepare questions, then checks drawings against the real wall and a skilled carpenter.
He explores **paid maintenance training** and robot trials, while acknowledging that capable robots could also take maintenance tasks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives David only until around 2031 before capable robots can perform his hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** with real placements, safety trials and honest job counts would support a credible transition.
